metaDescription: Six Fellow electric kettles compared: Stagg gooseneck, Corvo wide-spout and Clyde models, with notes on spouts, displays, scheduling and which to buy.
expertTake: The Stagg EKG Pro is the pick for anyone who brews pour-over, because its gooseneck and brew timer are the reason the line exists. The Clyde 1.5 liter is the value pick when you want a clean, drip-free boiler without the precision tooling. Anyone who only needs hot water for noodles or instant coffee should skip the whole brand and buy a plain kettle.
introParagraphs: This brand has built a small, design-led range of kettles that share a lot of DNA: a precise thermostat, a considered handle and a base that looks as good as it works. The real choice inside the range is the spout, the display and how much body you need.

We sorted the lineup by what each model is for rather than by finish. A gooseneck suits slow pouring, a wide spout suits quick filling, and a boil-only body suits people who want clean lines and little else. Prices move and listings change, so confirm the details before buying.

products.name: Fellow Stagg EKG Pro Gooseneck Kettle 0.9L
products.description:
The Stagg EKG Pro is the model the whole line was designed around. Its gooseneck spout narrows the stream so you can wet a coffee bed slowly, and the full-color display and brew timer let you repeat a recipe. Temperature hold keeps the water at target while you pour, and scheduling can have it ready at a set time.

One drawback is that this is a specialist. At 0.9 liter it fills a few cups, so it is poor for a family pot or a ramen bowl. Next to the Corvo EKG Pro, the Stagg gives up fast filling and a wide pour for a thin, slow, controllable stream.

In year three, the attention goes to scale on the heating element and fingerprints on the finish. Descale on a schedule in hard water and wipe the body with a soft cloth. It is a counter fixture that rewards daily use, and an expensive ornament if you only pour coffee on weekends. Because the base holds the electronics and the heating contacts, lift the kettle straight up and avoid sliding it across the counter, which scratches the base and loosens the connection over time.
products.bestFor: Pour-over coffee drinkers who repeat a recipe daily.
pros: Gooseneck spout gives a slow, steady stream
Brew timer helps repeat a recipe
Temperature hold keeps water at target
Color display is easy to read
cons: Small 0.9 liter body fills few cups
Specialist design is poor for bulk boiling

products.name: Fellow Corvo EKG Pro Wide-Spout Kettle 0.9L

specList.label: Best use
specList.value: Tea, coffee and general hot water

products.description:
The Corvo EKG Pro keeps the same electronics as the Stagg but swaps the gooseneck for a wide spout. The listing positions it as an all-purpose kettle with to-the-degree temperature control and quick heating. Scheduling and a brew timer come over from the Pro platform.

The tradeoff is pour control. A wide spout fills a French press or a tea pot quickly, but it floods a pour-over filter. Beside the Clyde 1.5 liter, the Corvo has far more control and a smaller body, so the Clyde wins for volume while the Corvo wins for precision.

Ownership is the same as the Stagg: descale the element and keep the display clean. A wide spout is easier to rinse than a gooseneck, which makes the Corvo friendlier for tea, where leaves sometimes clog a narrow neck. It is the most versatile of the Pro models. If you also pour coffee through a cone, you can still do it, but expect to go slower and use a lighter touch on the handle, since the wide mouth releases water faster than a filter bed can absorb it.
products.bestFor: Households that brew tea and coffee and want one precise kettle.
pros: To-the-degree temperature control
Wide spout fills pots and presses fast
Same Pro display and scheduling
Easier to rinse than a gooseneck
cons: Wide spout is poor for pour-over
Premium cost for a smaller kettle

products.name: Fellow Stagg EKG Pro Studio Gooseneck 0.9L
products.description:
The Studio edition carries the same precision as the standard Stagg EKG Pro, with a glass base and metal accents on top. The gooseneck, temperature control and scheduling are unchanged. The change is aesthetic and tactile, not functional.

The catch is that you pay for appearance. A glass base is a more fragile surface than the standard finish, and its looks are the reason to choose it. Compared with the standard Stagg EKG Pro, the Studio costs more for the same brewing performance.

Care means protecting the glass and wiping fingerprints. Descaling is the same as other models. Choose the Studio only if the base is a visible part of your counter. If you move the kettle between a shelf and a counter often, a standard finish is the safer match, because a glass base takes a knock worse than a metal one and a replacement base is a significant part of the original cost.
products.bestFor: Pour-over drinkers who care how the kettle looks.
pros: Same precision as the standard Pro
Glass base and metal accents look premium
Gooseneck for slow pouring
Full-color display and scheduling
cons: Costs more for the same brewing function

products.name: Fellow Corvo EKG Pro Studio Kettle 0.9L
products.description:
This is the Corvo EKG Pro in its Studio dress, with a glass base, metal accents and a matte finish. The wide spout, temperature control and brew timer are the same as the standard Corvo. The extra cost is for the look.

The tradeoff is again style over function. Beside the standard Corvo Pro, the Studio brews no better, so it only makes sense if you want the finish. Against the Stagg Studio, it pours wider and faster.

Care follows the other Pro models: descale and wipe. The glass base asks for more careful handling. Picture it as a good gift or a counter statement more than a performance upgrade. Households with several people sharing a kitchen should note that the matte surface collects oils from hands, so keep a microfiber cloth nearby, and avoid abrasive pads that burnish the finish in patches.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the Corvo's versatility in a premium finish.
pros: Same all-purpose Corvo performance
Glass base and metal accents look refined
Wide spout speeds up filling
Full-color display and brew timer
cons: Costs more for no brewing gain

products.name: Fellow Corvo EKG Stainless Tea Kettle
products.description:
The original Corvo EKG is a stainless teapot-shaped kettle that pairs a minimalist look with temperature control and quick heating. It lacks the full-color display and brew timer of the Pro line, so it is simpler to operate. That simplicity is the selling point.

The tradeoff is feature depth. Against the Corvo EKG Pro, it gives up the scheduling and timer, and gains a cleaner, quieter user experience. It also has a lower cost of ownership because there is less electronics to fail.

Care is routine: descale and wipe the stainless. It suits someone who wants the brand's design without the digital extras. With fewer electronics there is less to reset after a power cut, and a simple control scheme means anyone in the household can use it without reading a manual, which matters in a shared kitchen.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want clean design and simple temperature control.
pros: Stainless body is durable
Simple controls with little to learn
Quick heating for tea and coffee
Minimalist look fits any counter
cons: Display is less capable than Pro models

products.name: Fellow Clyde 1.5L Drip-Free Stainless Kettle

specList.label: Best use
specList.value: French press, ramen and family tea

products.description:
The Clyde is the volume model of the range: a 1.5 liter stainless kettle with a short angled spout built to pour cleanly without dribbling down the side. The listing says it boils enough water for a full French press or a bowl of ramen, which is exactly the job a 0.9 liter Pro cannot do. It leaves out the screen and the scheduling and keeps the brand's tidy look.

The cost of that simplicity is precision. There is no gooseneck and no timer, so it is not a pour-over tool, and the stainless interior may show a visible manufacturing seam according to the listing, which is cosmetic. Placed next to the Corvo EKG Pro, the Clyde holds about two thirds more water and costs less, but gives up to-the-degree control.

Everyday ownership is easy: a short spout rinses clean, and stainless hides scale better than glass. Descale on a schedule in hard water and wipe the outside. It is the sensible Fellow for anyone who boils more than a mug at a time.
products.bestFor: Families and anyone who needs a bigger, cleaner-pouring boiler.
pros: 1.5 liter body fills a French press fully
Short angled spout pours without dripping
304 stainless interior is easy to keep clean
Lowest cost entry in the brand's range
cons: No timer, scheduling or precise control

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Stagg models use a gooseneck that slows the stream for pour-over, while the Corvo models use a wide spout that fills quickly. A gooseneck is excellent for a filter cone and awkward for a pot. Pick by how you pour, and remember that a wide spout like the Corvo EKG Pro cannot match the Stagg's thin stream no matter how steady your hand is. A useful check is how the spout behaves at a low tilt: a true gooseneck keeps a thin stream even when the kettle is nearly level, while a wide spout releases a sheet of water as soon as you tip it. Beginners sometimes buy a gooseneck and find it awkward for filling a mug, which is why the Corvo line exists.

The Pro and Studio models add a full-color display, brew timer and scheduling. The original Corvo EKG leaves those out. If you follow a recipe with a timed bloom, the timer is useful; if you only want hot water, it is wasted. Ask whether you would actually program a wake-up boil before paying for it.

The Studio editions of the Stagg and Corvo add a glass base and metal accents without changing brewing performance. They cost more for looks. Choose them only if the base sits where guests see it, and remember glass is more fragile than the standard finish.

Most of the range is 0.9 liter, enough for about three and a half cups. The Clyde at 1.5 liters is the volume option for a French press or a bowl of ramen. Buying a 0.9 liter model for a family is the most common mistake in this range. Work out your typical batch first: a French press holds roughly a liter, which already exceeds the usable fill of a 0.9 liter kettle once you leave headroom below the max line. If you routinely fill a press or a large teapot, the Clyde saves a refill every time.

The Pro line advertises to-the-degree control, which matters for light roast coffee and green tea where a few degrees change the cup. The Clyde is a boil-oriented design with less emphasis on precision. If your recipe is exacting, choose Pro; if not, you are paying for accuracy you will not use.

Smaller bodies heat faster, so the 0.9 liter kettles reach temperature quickly at a modest fill. A full 1.5 liter Clyde takes longer. Ask whether the kettle will sit near a bedroom or study, since a quiet shut-off and a low-pitched heat-up are part of the premium appeal.

specDecoder.meaning: The ability to set a time for the kettle to start heating. It is a convenience for morning routines.
specDecoder.watchFor: Scheduling is a Pro feature and is not on the Clyde.

howWeEvaluated.title: Spout and pour
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared gooseneck against wide spout and drip-free designs. The Stagg ranks first for slow pouring and the Clyde for clean flow. The choice depends on your brewing method.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control and electronics
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed temperature control, hold, brew timer and scheduling. The Pro models lead, and the original Corvo EKG and Clyde score lower on features. We treated these as spec comparisons.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We balanced 0.9 liter bodies against the Clyde's 1.5 liters. Small bodies heat quickly but fill few cups. Large bodies serve groups.

howWeEvaluated.title: Finish and build
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared standard, matte and Studio glass-base finishes. Studio editions rank higher for look but lower for durability. Owner feedback patterns on fingerprints informed this.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value within the range
howWeEvaluated.description: We asked what each step up in price actually adds. The Studio editions add looks only, while the Pro models add features. The Clyde gives volume at the lowest tier.

cards.label: Stagg
cards.text: The Stagg models use a gooseneck for slow, precise pours onto a filter cone. They are the best match for pour-over coffee.

cards.label: Corvo
cards.text: The Corvo models use a wide spout that fills quickly, so they suit tea, French press and general use.

howToChoose.note: Choose Stagg for coffee precision; choose Corvo for versatility.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A gooseneck, accurate temperature hold and a timer so the bloom and pour are repeatable.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Stagg EKG Pro meets all of these, and the Stagg Studio adds a glass base for looks only.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want the Stagg's gooseneck and timer or the Corvo EKG Pro's scheduling and precision.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You want a clean boiler, where the Clyde 1.5 liter or the original Corvo EKG does the job.

maintenance.why: Scale insulates the heating element and slows reaching temperature. Citric acid per directions clears it.
Matte and brushed finishes show marks. A soft cloth restores the look without scratching.
Studio bases are glass and can chip on a hard knock. Place the kettle away from counter edges.
Water at the base interferes with power transfer. Wipe it dry.
Steam can leave film on the panel. Wipe gently so the numbers stay legible.

faq.q: What is the difference between Stagg and Corvo?
faq.a: The Stagg models use a gooseneck spout for slow pouring, while the Corvo models use a wide spout for fast filling. The electronics are similar on the Pro versions. Pick by how you pour.

faq.q: Is the Studio edition worth the extra cost?
faq.a: Only for looks. It adds a glass base and metal accents to the same brewing performance. If you value counter design it is a fair premium, otherwise buy the standard Pro.

faq.q: Which model is best for tea?
faq.a: The Corvo EKG Pro is the best match for mixed tea use because it combines precise temperature control with a wide spout. The original Corvo EKG is a simpler alternative.

faq.q: Are these kettles good for a family?
faq.a: Most are 0.9 liter, which is small. The Clyde at 1.5 liters is the family option. For a household that boils large pots often, the smaller models will feel limiting.

faq.q: Do these kettles use special descaling?
faq.a: No. Regular citric acid or vinegar descaling per the maker's directions works. Do it monthly in hard water, because scale on a small element affects heating.

faq.q: Is a premium kettle really better than a plain one?
faq.a: It boils no faster, but it holds temperature more precisely and pours more evenly. Whether that is worth it depends on your brewing. For plain hot water, it is not.
